articles.title: Updated: US Department of Homeland Security publishes rule to end Duration of Status for international students
articles.summary: The US Department of Homeland Security published a final rule on 22 July 2026 to eliminate Duration of Status (D/S) for F and J nonimmigrant students and their dependents. The rule reflects only minor revisions from DHS’s August 2025 proposal, despite extensive opposition from scientific, business, and higher education stakeholders.
articles.insight:
This rule signals potential long-term shifts in US appeal for international students, as stricter visa duration limits and increased compliance burdens may dampen demand—especially from risk-averse or academically mobile source markets—though immediate enrolment impacts remain uncertain amid broader geopolitical and economic factors.  
Admissions teams should track early application trends from key markets like India and China, monitor peer institutions’ US recruitment messaging, and assess whether complementary support services (e.g., visa advising, academic planning) need strengthening to offset perceived US regulatory complexity.

articles.title: England: Government “remains of the view” that the International Student Levy should go ahead; implementation planned for August 2028
articles.summary: The UK government confirmed in September 2025 that it would implement an International Student Levy of £925 per international student, to be charged as a flat fee to higher education providers. The levy is scheduled to take effect in August 2028, following its initial proposal in the May 2025 immigration white paper.
articles.insight:
The UK’s planned £925 International Student Levy—set for August 2028—may modestly dampen institutional willingness to recruit international students, particularly from lower-margin markets, though its direct impact on student demand or visa policy remains uncertain pending final implementation details and potential exemptions.  
Admissions teams should track how UK universities adjust recruitment targets, scholarship offerings, and agent partnerships in response to the levy, while benchmarking against tuition trends and policy shifts in Australia, Canada, and the US to assess relative value proposition changes for prospective students.

articles.title: UK unis join forces to offer study pathways for visa brake students
articles.summary: Nine UK universities are collaborating with the NGO Mosaik Education to offer remote postgraduate study pathways for international students from countries affected by the UK’s strict study visa pause. The initiative provides an alternative route for eligible students to begin their studies online before potentially transitioning to on-campus learning.
articles.insight:
This collaboration signals growing institutional adaptation to restrictive visa policies, potentially reflecting heightened student demand for flexible, lower-risk entry pathways amid global mobility uncertainty—though it remains unclear whether such models will shift broader enrolment preferences or merely serve as temporary workarounds.  
Admissions teams should monitor uptake and completion rates of these remote-to-on-campus pathways, as well as policy developments in key source markets, to assess whether similar hybrid models could strengthen recruitment resilience without compromising academic integrity or compliance.
